extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent attorneys, judges, and practitioners dealing with patent renewals/extensions
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of legal and procedural criteria governing extensions (renewals) of patent terms under the 1836 Act and related provisions, and the proper construction of who benefits (patentee vs. assignees/grantees). Focuses on application requirements, evidentiary showings, statutory interpretation rules, and limits on assignees' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply for extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The application for an extension must be made by the patentee (not any assignee) to the commissioner of the patent office, setting forth the grounds thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that the word 'patentee' is used as equivalent to 'inventor' and that the law looked to him as the sole object of its bounty (rewarding his time, ingenuity, and expense). Later statutory amendments (e.g., 1837) changed some issuance rules, but the 1836 section contemplates application by the inventor/patentee while the original patent term is still running.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of application — must be before original expiry
rubrics_metrics.description: No extension of a patent shall be granted after the expiration of the term for which it was originally issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proviso contemplates the application 'while the term of the original patent is yet running' and expressly declares extensions cannot be granted post-expiration. This timing requirement is central to construing other clauses in the section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition and hearing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The secretary of state, the commissioner of the patent office, and the solicitor of the treasury shall constitute a board to hear and decide upon the evidence produced for and against the extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute prescribes notice and a hearing before this governmental board; the board must examine receipts/expenditures and other evidence before deciding whether to extend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirement — sworn accounting of value, receipts, expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is required to furnish to the board a statement in writing, under oath, of the ascertained value of the invention, and of his receipts and expenditures, sufficient to exhibit a true and faithful account of loss and profit accruing from or by reason of the said invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accounting enables the board to determine whether the patentee failed to attain reasonable remuneration; the statute contemplates a detailed, sworn financial showing of profit and loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive standard for granting extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The board must be 'to the full and entire satisfaction' convinced, 'having due regard to the public interest therein,' that it is just and proper that the term of the patent should be extended by reason of the patentee, without neglect or fault on his part, having failed to attain from the use and sale of his invention a reasonable remuneration for the time, ingenuity, and expense bestowed upon the same, and the introduction thereof into use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a discretionary, fact-intensive standard focused on compensation of the inventor; public interest is also a consideration. The patentee's lack of neglect/fault and failure to obtain reasonable remuneration are key factual predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of benefit to assignees and grantees
rubrics_metrics.description: 'And the benefit of such renewal shall extend to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented, to the extent of their respective interests therein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clause is interpreted narrowly: the benefit extends only to the assignees' or grantees' existing interests in the patent/right to use as they stood under the original patent (no enlargement beyond what was granted). If the original assignment limited interest to the original term, the assignee gets no extra benefit in the renewed term unless the assignment expressly or by necessary implication conferred such future interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignees' rights limited to what assignor could assign
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee's or grantee's interest in the renewed patent cannot exceed what the grantor/assignor then possessed and was capable of assigning; courts should not presume they received compensation for future, contingent rights unless explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against construing assignments to transfer prospective/contingent future renewals absent express words or necessary implication; doing so would improperly transfer the government's intended bounty for the inventor to an assignee who paid nothing for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent interests and change of character upon vesting
rubrics_metrics.description: A contingent interest in the new term (derived from a provision in an assignment under the old term) rests in contract until the contingency occurs and may be enforceable in equity; the clause might operate to change the nature of such contingent interest into a vested legal right after the contingency happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recognizes a limited role for the clause here: it may remove doubt about the character of the interest after the contingency, but it does not create the contingent right (which depends on contract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/linguistic limits on creating exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause's wording — 'assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented' — does not, in terms, confer an exclusive right to make and vend; exclusive monopolies in patents are created only by the usual formula 'the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using, and vending.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not read a complete monopoly into a clause that only references a right 'to use' without the customary explicit language granting exclusivity; legislative drafting conventions matter for conferring monopoly privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal as a new grant vesting exclusive rights in patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension under the eighteenth section is a new grant of the exclusive right or monopoly in the subject of the invention for seven years; rights of assignees/grantees under the old term terminate at the end of the original term and reinvest in the patentee unless the original grant expressly covered future renewals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the date of the new grant the patentee again possesses 'the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using and vending' the invention; purchasers/users in possession are affected unless covered by the qualifying clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause meant to protect existing users/purchasers to extent of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualifying clause is naturally read as pointing to those who were in the use of the patented article at the time of the renewal, intending to restore or save to them that right to use which otherwise would have been vested exclusively in the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting 'thing patented' and 'right to use' in context suggests the clause protects practical users (e.g., purchasers of machines in use) by preserving their ability to use existing machines to the extent of their interests at the time of extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of statutory construction for doubtful phraseology
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statutory words or phraseology are obscure or doubtful, the intention of the lawmakers should be sought from context, general provisions, and policy of the patent law to fix and control meaning so as to reconcile it with the general policy of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly applies this rule: ambiguous language should be construed in light of the section's object (rewarding the inventor) and the overall patent system; constructions repugnant to the statute's purpose require very explicit statutory language to be adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should avoid constructions that subvert legislative purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should hesitate to adopt constructions that are harsh or unjust in consequence, or that subvert the whole object and purpose of the enactment, unless the statute uses the most fixed and positive terms to justify such a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary stresses that giving assignees full renewal benefits contrary to the section's intent (to remunerate inventors) would be unjust and would require explicit words; judicial parsimony is advised when a construction would transfer the government's bounty away from the inventor.
